Model Response:

The Case for Extending Voting Rights to Long-Term Noncitizen Residents: Democracy Demands Inclusion

Introduction

In the autumn of 2022, an estimated 15.4 million legal permanent residents lived in the United States, many of them for decades—paying taxes, raising families, serving in the military, building businesses, and contributing to their communities in every measurable way. They attend school board meetings in their children's districts. They obey federal, state, and local laws. They contribute to Social Security and Medicare—programs from which many of them will never collect benefits. Yet when Election Day arrives, they are turned away from the polls, their voices silenced by a single missing document: a certificate of naturalization. This exclusion is not merely an oversight in democratic design. It is an ongoing violation of the foundational principle upon which American governance was built—that those who are subject to the laws of a polity must have a voice in shaping them. The time has come to extend full voting rights in U.S. elections to legal permanent residents and other long-term noncitizen residents, not as a radical experiment, but as a principled return to the deepest logic of representative democracy.

This essay argues that granting voting rights to long-term noncitizen residents is morally justified, historically grounded, practically beneficial, and constitutionally permissible. Far from diluting the meaning of citizenship, such an extension would honor the meaning of democracy itself.

I. The Foundational Principle: No Taxation Without Representation—and Beyond

The rallying cry of the American Revolution—"no taxation without representation"—is often invoked as a historical curiosity, a slogan suitable for placards and textbook headings but irrelevant to modern governance. This is a profound mistake. The principle it encodes is not merely historical; it is the irreducible core of democratic legitimacy. If government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed, then every person who is governed—who is subject to law, who pays taxes, who serves the commonweal—must have a channel through which to express or withhold that consent.

Consider what long-term noncitizen residents actually do in American society. According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, undocumented immigrants alone paid an estimated $11.7 billion in state and local taxes in 2019, while legal permanent residents contribute billions more. They pay federal income tax, payroll tax, sales tax, and property tax—often through rent, which constitutes a pass-through of property tax obligations. They are subject to military Selective Service registration. They are bound by every criminal statute, civil regulation, and administrative rule that citizens face. In the language of political philosophy, they are not merely affected by government; they are governed. John Stuart Mill argued that "the suffrage... should be conceded to every one who has to bear his share of the common burdens." By this standard alone, the disenfranchisement of taxpaying, law-abiding residents is indefensible.

Moreover, the "no taxation without representation" principle is not limited to fiscal obligations. It extends to every form of civic obligation. Long-term residents serve on juries (where permitted), comply with environmental regulations, adhere to zoning laws, and submit to the authority of inspectors, licensing boards, and regulatory agencies. They are, in the fullest sense, members of the political community—except for the one attribute that supposedly defines membership: the right to vote. This is not a coherent theory of democratic inclusion. It is an accident of birth dressed up as political philosophy.

II. A Historical Tradition of Noncitizen Voting

One of the most powerful arguments for extending voting rights to noncitizens is that the United States has done so before—extensively, and for most of its history. The notion that voting has always been reserved for citizens is a myth, and dispelling it reveals that the current regime of universal citizen-only suffrage is the aberration, not the norm.

From the founding of the Republic through the mid-twentieth century, more than forty states and territories at various times allowed noncitizens to vote in some or all elections. In the early Republic, several states permitted propertied white male immigrants to vote, often after a brief period of residency. The logic was pragmatic and philosophical alike: the nation needed to attract settlers and signal that membership in the political community was earned through contribution, not merely inherited through birth. As the political historian Leon Aylsworth documented in a landmark 1931 study, noncitizen voting was practiced across the country for over a century and a half, with states such as Ohio (1802), Illinois (1818), Alabama (1819), and Michigan (1835) all extending the franchise to alien residents who declared their intention to become citizens.

The practice persisted well into the twentieth century. As late as 1926, Arkansas was the last state to eliminate noncitizen voting in state elections. The widespread rollback of alien suffrage was driven not by philosophical reflection but by xenophobic nationalism surrounding World War I and the anti-immigrant fervor of the 1920s. The Chinese Exclusion Act, "America First" chauvinism, and racial panic conspired to narrow the boundaries of political belonging. The retreat from noncitizen voting was, in other words, a product of prejudice rather than principle. Recovering this history does not mean replicating every feature of early American suffrage policy—many of those regimes were deeply exclusionary along lines of race, gender, and property. But it does mean recognizing that the current exclusion of long-term noncitizens from the franchise is neither historically necessary nor philosophically original.

Today, several jurisdictions have begun to reverse the trend. As of 2024, eleven municipalities in Maryland—including Takoma Park and Barnesville—allow noncitizen residents to vote in local elections. San Francisco permits noncitizen parents to vote in school board elections. In 2021, New York City passed legislation granting green card holders and individuals with work authorization the right to vote in municipal elections (though legal challenges have since complicated implementation). These measures reflect a growing recognition that local democracy should include all local stakeholders—and that the historical precedent is firmly on the side of inclusion.

III. The Argument from Affected Interests

Contemporary political philosophy offers a powerful framework for evaluating democratic inclusion: the "all-affected interests" principle. In its simplest form, the principle holds that anyone whose interests are significantly affected by a political decision should have a say in making that decision. This principle, articulated by scholars from Robert Dahl to more recent theorists like Sofia Näsström and Arash Abizadeh, provides the most compelling justification for extending the franchise to noncitizen residents.

Consider the breadth of policy decisions that directly shape the lives of legal permanent residents. Immigration policy determines whether their families can be reunified. Tax policy determines how much of their income is taken by the state. Education policy determines the quality of their children's schooling. Criminal justice policy determines the conditions under which they might be detained or deported. Healthcare policy determines whether they can access medical treatment. Labor law determines the protections they receive at work. Environmental policy determines the air they breathe and the water they drink. Housing policy determines where and how they live. The list is nearly infinite, because modern government touches virtually every aspect of life.

It is true that citizens, too, are affected by all of these policies. But the scope of affected interests is precisely what grounds democratic claims—it does not require that the affected party be uniquely or exclusively affected. A citizen who does not have children in public schools is still affected by education policy; we do not therefore disenfranchise her. The relevant question is whether a person's interests are significantly and legitimately affected by political decisions, and the answer for long-term noncitizen residents is unambiguously yes.

The "all-affected interests" principle also exposes the arbitrariness of using citizenship as a proxy for affectedness. Citizens who have never lived in the United States and have no intention of doing so can retain their citizenship and, in some contexts, their ability to vote in federal elections. Meanwhile, a husband green card holder who has lived in Ohio for twenty-five years, worked for a public university, paid taxes, and sent all three children to public schools has no vote in any election. The disconnect between affectedness and enfranchisement is not a minor gap; it is a canyon.

IV. The Democratic Dividend: Why Inclusion Strengthens Governance

Opponents of noncitizen voting often raise the specter of democratic dilution—the fear that extending the franchise to noncitizens will dilute the voting power of citizens, distort electoral outcomes, or degrade the meaning of civic belonging. These concerns, while understandable, are both empirically unsupported and philosophically shallow.

First, the empirical evidence from jurisdictions that have adopted noncitizen voting is reassuring. In Takoma Park, Maryland—one of the longest-running examples of noncitizen voting in the United States—the inclusion of noncitizen residents in municipal elections has not produced any of the catastrophic outcomes opponents predicted. Noncitizen voter turnout has been modest but meaningful. Electoral outcomes have not been radically transformed. The quality of governance has not declined. If anything, studies of local noncitizen voting suggest that it increases civic engagement, strengthens community cohesion, and makes local government more responsive to the full diversity of its constituency.

Second, the argument from "dilution" is logically inconsistent with the broader history of franchise expansion in the United States. Every major extension of voting rights—to non-property-owning white men, to Black men after the Civil War, to women, to eighteen-year-olds—was met with predictions of democratic collapse. None of those predictions came true. In every case, the expansion of the franchise made American democracy more legitimate, more responsive, and more stable. The fears that accompany democratization are perennial; their falsity is equally perennial.

Third, including noncitizens in the electorate would improve policy outcomes by ensuring that the perspectives of a substantial and growing portion of the population are represented in the political process. When a significant bloc of residents is disenfranchised, politicians have fewer incentives to attend to their needs. The result is predictable: policies that exploit, neglect, or harm noncitizen populations with minimal political consequence. Extending the franchise would create accountability where it is currently lacking, forcing elected officials to consider the interests of all their constituents, not merely those with naturalization papers.

Research by political scientists supports this analysis. Studies of local immigrant integration have found meaningful positive effects of political participation: higher trust in public institutions, greater use of public services, enhanced sense of belonging, and lower crime rates. The immigrant rights scholar Ron Hayduk, author of Democracy for All: Restoring Immigrant Voting Rights in the United States, has argued that the enfranchisement of noncitizens is not a threat to democracy but an investment in it—an opportunity to deepen civic culture, reduce inequality, and make government more responsive to those it governs.

V. The "Stakeholder" Argument: Community Membership Beyond Citizenship

One of the most intuitive arguments for noncitizen voting is also one of the most powerful: long-term residents are already members of their communities in every meaningful sense except the political one. The political theorist Rainer Bauböck has advanced a "stakeholder" theory of political membership, arguing that those who have a substantive stake in a community's future—through residence, employment, family ties, and social participation—should have a say in its governance. This theory does not deny the significance of citizenship; it simply recognizes that citizenship is not the only form of legitimate political belonging.

Think of what it means to be a long-term noncitizen resident in practical terms. It means owning or renting a home, contributing to a neighborhood, participating in religious and civic organizations, volunteering for local causes, coaching children's sports teams, attending PTA meetings, reporting emergencies to 911, and trusting local police to provide protection. It means being embedded in a web of social relationships, obligations, and expectations that is indistinguishable from the web in which citizens are embedded. The noncitizen resident is not a guest in the community; she is a member of it.

The political philosopher Judith Shklar's influential concept of "standing" is illuminating here. Shklar argued that American citizenship is, at its core, about social standing—about being recognized as a full and equal member of the political community. To deny long-term noncitizens the vote is to send a message, however unintentional, that they are second-class members of the community—subject to its laws but excluded from its governance, contributing to its prosperity but denied a share in its self-determination. This is not merely a theoretical concern; it is a lived reality that breeds alienation, distrust, and disengagement—precisely the opposite of what a healthy democracy requires.

VI. Addressing the Counterarguments

"Only citizens should vote; citizenship is the basis of political membership."

This argument has a certain surface plausibility, but it collapses under scrutiny. Citizenship is not a natural kind; it is a legal status, and the boundaries of that status are drawn by political choices that can be made differently. For most of American history, the requirements for naturalization were minimal, and the pathway to citizenship was widely understood as a reward for contribution and integration. Today, the pathway to naturalization is long, expensive, Kafkaesque, and in many cases effectively closed. The average wait time for naturalization in many U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services offices exceeds two years, and the backlog of applications has at times surpassed 700,000. Application costs—$725 per person, plus legal fees that often total thousands of dollars—place citizenship beyond the reach of many long-term residents. The idea that citizenship is a straightforward and accessible marker of political membership is a fiction; for many, it is an impossible dream.

Moreover, the argument that only citizens should vote proves too much. If we take it to its logical conclusion, we should also deny voting rights to citizens who do not pay taxes, who are ignorant of public affairs, or who have no particular stake in the outcomes of elections. We do not do this, because we recognize that a healthy democracy requires a broad and inclusive franchise. The principle at work is not citizenship per se but membership in the political community, and long-term residents are manifestly members of that community.

"Noncitizens already have a pathway to citizenship; they should pursue that instead."

This argument conflates two distinct questions: (1) Should the pathway to citizenship be available? and (2) Should the absence of citizenship justify disenfranchisement? The answer to the first question is obviously yes; the United States should maintain and expand accessible pathways to naturalization. But the answer to the second question is no, because the right to participate in governance should not be contingent on the completion of a bureaucratic process that is, for many, prohibitively expensive, time-consuming, or legally impossible.

There are roughly 11 million undocumented immigrants in the United States, and a significant number of legal permanent residents who will never qualify for naturalization due to legal barriers, poverty, health conditions, or the sheer impossibility of navigating the immigration system. To say that these individuals should "just become citizens" if they want to vote is to erect a procedural barricade around democratic participation and then blame those who cannot surmount it. This is not a defense of democratic integrity; it is a defense of arbitrary exclusion.

"Noncitizens may have divided loyalties; they owe allegiance to their home countries."

This argument is both insulting and empirically false. Legal permanent residents have, by definition, been vetted by the U.S. government, have sworn an oath of allegiance as part of the naturalization process (or, for green card holders, have demonstrated commitment to the United States through years of residence and contribution), and have made their lives in this country. The notion that they harbor some kind of subversive loyalty is a xenophobic canard unsupported by any evidence. Indeed, many long-term residents who are eligible for naturalization have not pursued it because of practical barriers, not because of lack of commitment to the United States. And even for those who maintain cultural or emotional ties to their countries of origin—as citizens freely do every day—this dual belonging does not diminish their investment in their American communities or their right to participate in shaping the policies that govern their lives.

VII. The Constitutional and Legal Framework

Opponents of noncitizen voting sometimes invoke the Constitution as a barrier. But a careful reading of the constitutional text and Supreme Court precedent reveals the opposite: the Constitution not only permits noncitizen voting at the state and local levels but has been interpreted actively to protect such practices.

The Constitution does not grant an affirmative right to vote to any category of person; rather, it sets parameters—prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, sex, age (for those over eighteen), and failure to pay poll taxes—while delegating the administration of elections overwhelmingly to the states. Article I, Section 4 gives state legislatures primary authority over the "Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections," subject to congressional override. The Supreme Court has recognized this broad state authority to regulate the franchise within constitutional limits.

The Supreme Court's decision in Minor v. Happersett (1875), though later partially superseded by the Nineteenth Amendment, is relevant because it acknowledged that citizenship and voting are not coextensive. The Court held that while all citizens have a right to participate in the political community—a concept of broad belonging—voting is not a privilege or immunity of citizenship per se. This distinction between citizenship-as-belonging and voting-as-practice has been reaffirmed in subsequent jurisprudence, providing a constitutional foundation for state-level noncitizen voting.

The key equal protection question is whether disenfranchising noncitizens is rationally related to a legitimate governmental purpose. The Supreme Court, in cases such as Sugarman v. Dougall (1973) and Foley v. Connelie (1978), has recognized a "political function" exception to heightened equal protection scrutiny for public offices that are intimately connected with the process of democratic self-government. But the Court has also made clear that this exception does not extend automatically to the franchise itself. In Dunn v. Blumstein (1972), the Court protected voting as a fundamental right subject to strict scrutiny, and it has never held that the franchise may be denied to a class of resident stakeholders who are encompassed by the jurisdiction’s laws.

At the federal level, it is true that 18 U.S.C. § 611 makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. But this statute does not limit state or local authority, where most policy decisions that affect daily life are made. Extending the franchise to noncitizens in state, county, municipal, and school board elections is not only constitutionally permissible but is arguably the most impactful place to begin.

VIII. A Practical Path Forward

Extending voting rights to long-term noncitizen residents need not be accomplished all at once, nor need it be accomplished at every level of government simultaneously. A pragmatic, phased approach can build public support, generate evidence, and demonstrate the benefits of inclusion.

Step One: Universalize Local and Municipal Voting. The most immediate and politically feasible step is to extend the right to vote in local elections—city councils, county boards, school boards, and special districts—to all legal permanent residents. Local government is where policy decisions most directly affect daily life: zoning, policing, trash collection, road maintenance, public transportation, library funding, and, crucially, public education. Extending the franchise at this level would be consistent with the stakeholder principle and would build on the experiences of municipalities that have already taken this step.

Step Two: Expand to State Elections. As the success of local noncitizen voting becomes evident, states should consider extending the franchise to state elections as well. State government controls a vast array of policy areas—from taxation and healthcare to criminal justice and infrastructure—that profoundly affect long-term noncitizen residents. There is no principled reason why these residents should be governed by state officials they have no role in electing.

Step Three: Advocate for Federal Reform. Over the long term, Congress should consider amending or repealing the federal statute that prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. This would require a national conversation about the meaning of political membership in a diverse, dynamic society. Given the profound impact of federal policy on the lives of all U.S. residents, there is a strong moral case for including noncitizens in the selection of federal officeholders.

Step Four: Lower Barriers to Naturalization. While extending the franchise to noncitizens, the United States should simultaneously work to make the pathway to citizenship more accessible—reducing application fees, streamlining the process, and expanding eligibility. These two goals are complementary, not contradictory: a more inclusive democracy is one in which all residents have a voice regardless of citizenship status, and in which the transition from resident to citizen is achievable for all who desire it.

IX. The Moral Imperative

At its heart, the case for extending voting rights to long-term noncitizen residents is a moral one. It is the case for a democracy that lives up to its own ideals—a democracy that does not ration political voice based on the accidents of birth and bureaucratic status, but extends it to all who are genuinely and substantively part of the political community.

The United States has long prided itself on being a nation of immigrants—a place where newcomers arrive with little and, through hard work and sacrifice, build lives and communities that enrich the nation. But this pride rings hollow when the very people who have done the hard work, made the sacrifices, and built the communities are denied the most fundamental tool of democratic participation. A nation that praises immigrants' contributions while excluding them from the political process is not a nation that has reconciled its ideals with its practices. It is a nation that celebrates immigrants as workers and taxpayers while relegating them to permanent political silence.

The great civil rights struggles of American history were fought over precisely this question: who counts? Who is a full member of the political community? Who has the right to have a say in the decisions that shape their life? Each time the answer was expanded—to the propertyless, to formerly enslaved people, to women, to young people—the nation became more just and more democratic. Each time, opponents warned of dire consequences that never materialized. The current struggle over noncitizen voting is of a piece with this great tradition, and its resolution should be the same: inclusion over exclusion, principle over prejudice, democracy over parochialism.

Conclusion

The disenfranchisement of long-term noncitizen residents is not a feature of American democracy; it is a defect. It is a defect that contradicts the nation's most cherished ideals, violates its most basic principles of fair representation, and undermines the legitimacy of its governing institutions. The arguments in its favor—appeals to citizenship as a boundary, warnings about democratic dilution, fears of divided loyalty—cannot withstand philosophical, historical, or empirical scrutiny.

Extending voting rights to legal permanent residents and other long-term noncitizen residents is consistent with the principle of "no taxation without representation," grounded in the nation's own historical practices, supported by the best theories of democratic inclusion, and vindicated by the experience of jurisdictions that have already taken this step. It would strengthen American democracy by making it more inclusive, more accountable, and more just.

The question is not whether American democracy can afford to include noncitizen residents in the franchise. The question is whether American democracy can afford not to. The answer, rooted in the deepest traditions of American political thought and the lived reality of millions of governing-without-representing, is clear: democracy that excludes the governed is not democracy at all. It is time to bring it home.

The Principle of Stakeholder Democracy

The most compelling argument for resident voting is rooted in the concept of stakeholdership. Democracy is not merely a privilege bestowed upon those who hold a specific passport; it is a mechanism for governing communities where people live, work, raise families, and pay taxes. Long-term legal residents are deeply embedded in their communities. They pay federal, state, and local taxes—including income, property, and sales taxes—just as citizens do. By denying these residents a voice, the system implicitly suggests that their interests are secondary to those of citizens, despite their equal contribution to the communal good. Granting voting rights acknowledges that civic belonging is defined by participation and presence, not just legal status.

Historical Precedent and Constitutional Flexibility

Critics often argue that voting is inherently tied to citizenship, citing the U.S. Constitution. However, the Constitution does not explicitly restrict voting in state and local elections to citizens. In fact, for much of American history, noncitizen voting was common. From the founding era until the 1920s, nearly half of the states allowed noncitizens to vote in some or all elections. It was only with the rise of nativist sentiment and the passage of the Cable Act of 1922 that this practice largely disappeared.

Recognizing this history is crucial because it demonstrates that noncitizen voting is not a radical new idea, but a restoration of a traditional American practice. Furthermore, because the Constitution leaves the determination of voter eligibility for state and local elections largely to the states, expanding these rights does not require a constitutional amendment. It requires political will and legislative action at the state and municipal levels, similar to recent movements in cities like Takoma Park, Maryland, and San Francisco, California, which have already extended voting rights to noncitizens in school board or local elections. These experiments have shown that such policies are administratively feasible and do not disrupt electoral integrity.

Fostering Integration and Civic Engagement

Opponents of resident voting often claim that it discourages naturalization. However, evidence suggests the opposite: inclusive policies foster deeper civic engagement and accelerate integration. When residents feel that their voices matter, they are more likely to engage with civic life, attend town halls, join community organizations, and stay informed about local issues. A common counter-argument is that voting is a sovereign right reserved for those who have pledged ultimate allegiance to the nation through citizenship. It simply recognizes that a neighbor who has lived in a community for ten years, pays taxes, and sends their children to local schools has a vested interest in the quality of those schools and the safety of those streets, regardless of their passport. Differentiating between local and national voting rights allows for a nuanced approach that respects both the unique bond of citizenship and the practical realities of community membership.
